units.translation: But when I hold my night-wandering, dewy bed, not visited by dreams—for fear stands by me instead of sleep, so that I cannot firmly close my eyelids in sleep. Thus M. Aeschylus would have written absurdly if he had added that useless ἐμήν [my], and that too placed at the beginning of the verse, but had omitted the apodosis of the words εὐτ᾽ ἂν – ἔχω [whenever – I hold], which the interpreters excuse, using here as elsewhere not infrequently more obscure reasoning, which none of the Athenian spectators would have guessed. The poet wrote not ἐμὴν [my], with which the interpolator filled the gap of two syllables (no less unskillfully than in Prometheus v. 1006 ἐμαῖς [my] was inserted when κέαρ [heart] had fallen out at the end of the preceding verse), but λύζω [I hiccup], a word used by Hippocrates, Aristophanes Ach. 690, and other ancients: see Thes. vol. 5 p. 418. For, as Aristotle observed in Problems 33, 13, οἱ φοβούμενοι καὶ οἱ ῥιγοῦντες λύζουσιν [those who are afraid and those who shiver hiccup], both of which apply to this watchman, who is exposed to the night cold and himself says that he is tormented by constant fear, and Aristotle's observation seems to have been taken from this very passage of Aeschylus, since λύζειν [to hiccup] in all other passages of writers known to us has the simple meaning of hiccuping, without the notion of cold, which is peculiar to the Aeschylean passage. With λύζω [I hiccup] restored, which signifies an inarticulate sobbing, the text aptly continues, ὅταν δ᾽ ἀείδειν ἢ μινύρεσθαι δοκῶ [but whenever I seem to sing or hum]. The scholiast had the common reading, who on the words φόβος γάρ [for fear] noted, ἢ περισσὸς ὁ γάρ, ἢ λείπει τὸ ἀλύω [either γάρ is redundant, or ἀλύω is missing], who came very close to the true reading λύζω [I hiccup].
A surname of Apollo, about whose origin different stories are told; see Thes. vol. 5 p. 422 and Welcker, Mythology of the Greeks vol. 1 p. 476-482.
And you, Lycean lord, be Lycean to the hostile army, just as in the following verses Diana is invoked to shoot arrows against the enemies besieging the city.

Where the murder of Agamemnon is being prepared in the palace, Cassandra cries out: ὀτοτοῖ, Λύκει᾿ Ἄπολλον, οἴ ἐγὼ ἐγώ [Alas, Lycean Apollo, woe is me, woe is me!]. This two-footed lioness (Clytemnestra), sleeping with a wolf (Aegisthus) in the absence of the noble lion (Agamemnon), will kill me, wretched one.
Omitting the god's name, Suppl. 686: εὐμενὴς δ᾽ ὁ Λύκειος ἔστω πάσᾳ νεολαίᾳ [May the Lycean be gracious to all the young people].
They dragged him upward like wolves.
